items.note: Checked at 4e96e5c0140ee973b11b6b17752964b926f8f02c. lab.json still declares common-api-security-risks-owasp#o3, and README Task 7 step 6 (lines 116-120) still carries it as an executable act: for each of the five practices the objective names, the learner writes the attacker request that practice is there to answer, and task7ShowsTheAttackEachPracticeStops sends it to the finished app and judges it from runtime behaviour; the risk names stay in the collapsed read-after block (lines 141-150). Critic runs this round on fresh git-archive copies of 4e96e5c0140ee973b11b6b17752964b926f8f02c (JDK 25.0.5, Maven 3.9.16, offline, mvn -q -o test from starter/). The shipped starter ran 10 tests, failed exactly the 9 lab.json failingTests, kept defaultProfileSendsNoCorsHeaders passing, and the step 6 check named Task 3 first. The private completion exited 0 with no output, surefire 2, 1 and 7 tests as in expected/test-summary.txt (about 13 s wall time here). My own alternative-correct set (a stolen-table login as a customer, the other customer on the real admin action, ADMIN with a negative id written in lower case with two spaces, the other customer reading her own booking, a customer asking for a booking that is not hers) passed; a second set with the hashing row as Grace passed with the step 6 test run alone. Five non-passing sets, my own edits, failed every wrong row in one run each with a true row-specific reason: a real password, an unknown account and a plain request for hashing; an anonymous caller, ADMIN, and the reading's admin-users DELETE that this API lacks for role checks; a login (now told it was refused by the password check), an anonymous bad id, a body-less registration and a 100-character login for validation; the public workshop list, another customer's booking and an anonymous request for the DTO; a validation error, an anonymous request, a failed login, a {placeholder} path and a non-numeric id for safe error bodies. So a row passes only when its practice answers the request, and I judge #o3 practised. The loop-8 side effect is now gone: a validation row built directly with the Attack record as an anonymous blank-field registration fails, because registration now answers its own constraint errors through BindingResult and no exception is resolved; its message (no Bean Validation constraint rejected this request) is too strong for that one form, since the shipped @NotBlank did reject it, but the form lies outside the documented helpers and README line 120 asks for the learner's own constraint, so it is noted, not filed.

Checked at 4e96e5c0140ee973b11b6b17752964b926f8f02c, re-judged on the current bytes rather than inherited. No table pairs a practice with an answer; each row's verdict is computed at runtime from the response, the resolved exception, the Booking fields and the ApiErrors handler types, and the failure line is the problem list (line 215), so no failure points at an answer line. Loop 9 adds a roles-claim prerequisite (lines 246-255), a password-check message (lines 390-392) and a probe that sends a marker exception through Spring MVC's handlerExceptionResolver for the booking handler (lines 477-517); none states a passing request beyond what loop 8 already held (the probe's request line for a missing booking existed at loop 8). Merits verdict on the brief's question (can step 6 be passed without making the connection), stated at full extent: learner-readable cues exist for every row. task7ServesOnlyTheCallersOwnBooking puts Grace's own booking beside 'sees only the response fields' (lines 173-179), another customer's booking beside 'the body reveals nothing internal' (lines 180-186) and a zero id beside 'a bad id is the client's mistake' (lines 189-191); task2 puts a customer on the admin path beside 'the wrong role 403' (lines 96-100); the STOLEN constant and its Javadoc cover the hashing row. My own set built from those shapes passed. README Task 7 steps 2 to 4 state the same effects openly. So step 6 is a scaffolded retrieval act, not discovery: what the learner must still do is take each practice and decide which attacker request it answers, then write that request in the attacker's form against the right caller; my wrong sets show the plausible misplacements (a real-password login for hashing, a missing admin action or the wrong caller for role checks, a login or anonymous request for validation, another customer's booking for the DTO, a validation error for safe errors) each fail with a true reason. Choosing which request goes with which practice is the connection #o3 names (connect practices to the risks they reduce, the risks themselves being read after the run), so I keep this resolved; the cues make it easier, they do not answer it for the learner, and the per-practice choice is still what is graded.

Checked at 4e96e5c0140ee973b11b6b17752964b926f8f02c. Critic probe test added only to a scratch copy of the completion (POST /auth/register over MockMvc): registering admin with an attacker's password returned 409 and the real admin login still returned 200; a new name returned 201. The takeover this finding filed stays closed under the loop-9 BindingResult rewrite. The residual noted since loop 6 (201 versus 409 reveals which names exist) is unchanged and routed to the technology SME; no step 6 verdict depends on it. Note for the technology SME, not filed: loop 9 adds @Size(max = 72) with the Javadoc 'bcrypt reads at most 72 bytes, so a password over 72 characters is refused too'. The sentence is literally true, but the cap does not cover a password of at most 72 characters and more than 72 UTF-8 bytes; under MockMvc, 72 ASCII characters returned 201, 73 returned 400, and 40 accented characters (80 bytes) and 30 emoji (60 characters, 120 bytes) passed the constraint and ended in an unhandled IllegalArgumentException from Spring Security 7.1.2's BCrypt ('password cannot be more than 72 bytes'), nothing stored. No README step, test or helper posts to /auth/register (login() goes to /auth/token), so no learner on the documented path reaches it; I did not run the live app.

Checked at 4e96e5c0140ee973b11b6b17752964b926f8f02c. handlerEchoesExceptionText (lines 477-517) no longer calls ApiErrors methods by reflection; it builds a marker exception of the failing type and resolves it through the application's handlerExceptionResolver for the booking handler, with a JWT authentication in the security context and as the request principal, then reads the written body and error message. I first checked it is not vacuous: my edits of the completion's ApiErrors, each run with SecurityLabTest and OwnBookingTest, that copy the exception text into the response all failed only with 'answeredBySafeErrorBodies: the error body still reveals the exception': a one-parameter ProblemDetail handler, a handler taking JwtAuthenticationToken and dereferencing it (the loop-8 residual, now caught), one taking @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt, one taking HttpServletRequest, one returning a ResponseEntity of a Map, and an advice that extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler (which the ProblemDetail page mentions) with an echoing handler. Controls passed: the completion, a fixed-detail handler that names the caller through a Principal parameter, and the completion's advice extended from ResponseEntityExceptionHandler. Reasoned from the code, not run: a handler that itself throws inside the probe counts as not echoing; on the documented path the same handler would also fail the real request, which the row reports separately.
